entries.c165726459865eb4b1c8a03e1fc8438f8e828139: <div sID="gen20907" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Zech.9" sID="Zech.9"/> <div eID="gen20907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20908" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20909" type="x-p"/> At this chapter begins another sermon, which is continued to the end of <reference osisRef="Zech.11.1-Zech.11.17">ch. xi.</reference> It is called, "The burden of the word of the Lord," for every word of God has weight in it to those who regard it, and will be a heavy weight upon those who do not, a dead weight. Here is, I. A prophecy against the Jews' unrighteous neighbours—the Syrians, Tyrians, Philistines, and others (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.1-Zech.9.6">ver. 1-6</reference>), with an intimation of mercy to some of them, in their conversion (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.7">ver. 7</reference>), and a promise of mercy to God's people, in their protection, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.8">ver. 8</reference>. II. A prophecy of their righteous King, the Messiah, and his coming, with a description of him (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">ver. 9</reference>) and of his kingdom, the nature and extent of it, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">ver. 10</reference>. III. An account of the obligation the Jews lay under to Christ for their deliverance out of their captivity in Babylon, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.11-Zech.9.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. IV. A prophecy of the victories and successes God would grant to the Jews over their enemies, as typical of our great deliverance by Christ, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.13-Zech.9.15">ver. 13-15</reference>. V. A promise of great plenty, and joy, and honour, which God had in reserve for his people (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.16-Zech.9.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>), which was written for their encouragement.
entries.15912b7b8be1b54f64586f1042cd8caab91ef922: <div eID="gen20909" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20908" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prophecy against Syria; Prophecy against the Enemies of Israel; Judgments and Mercies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  510.)</title> <div sID="gen20910" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden of the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the rest thereof: when the eyes of man, as of all the tribes of Israel, <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> toward the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> And Hamath also shall border thereby; Tyrus, and Zidon, though it be very wise. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Tyrus did build herself a strong hold, and heaped up silver as the dust, and fine gold as the mire of the streets. <hi type="super">4</hi> Behold, the Lord will cast her out, and he will smite her power in the sea; and she shall be devoured with fire. <hi type="super">5</hi> Ashkelon shall see <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and fear; Gaza also <hi type="italic">shall see it,</hi> and be very sorrowful, and Ekron; for her expectation shall be ashamed; and the king shall perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited. <hi type="super">6</hi> And a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines. <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will take away his blood out of his mouth, and his abominations from between his teeth: but he that remaineth, even he, <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> for our God, and he shall be as a governor in Judah, and Ekron as a Jebusite. <hi type="super">8</hi> And I will encamp about mine house because of the army, because of him that passeth by, and because of him that returneth: and no oppressor shall pass through them any more: for now have I seen with mine eyes. <div eID="gen20910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20911" type="x-p"/> After the precious promises we had in the foregoing chapter of favour to God's people, their persecutors, who hated them, come to be reckoned with, those particularly that bordered close upon them. <div eID="gen20911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20912" type="x-p"/> I. The Syrians had been bad neighbours to Israel, and God had a controversy with them. The word of the Lord shall be a <hi type="italic">burden in the land of Hadrach,</hi> that is, of <hi type="italic">Syria,</hi> but it does not appear why it was so called. That that kingdom is meant is plain, because Damascus, the metropolis of that kingdom, is said to be the <hi type="italic">rest</hi> of this burden; that is, the judgments here threatened shall light and lie upon that city. Those are miserable upon whom the burden of the word of the Lord rests, upon whom <hi type="italic">the wrath of God abides</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.36">John iii. 36</reference>); for it is a weight that they can neither shake off nor bear up under. There are those whom God <hi type="italic">causes his fury to rest</hi> upon. Those whom the wrath of God makes its mark it will be sure to hit; those whom it makes its rest it will be sure to sink. And the reason of this burden's resting on Damascus is because <hi type="italic">the eyes of man, as of all the tribes of Israel</hi> (or rather, <hi type="italic">even of all the tribes of Israel</hi>), are <hi type="italic">towards the Lord,</hi> because the people of God by faith and prayer look up to him for succour and relief and depend upon him to take their part against their enemies. Note, It is a sign that God is about to appear remarkably for his people when he raises their believing expectations from him and dependence upon him, and when by his grace he turns them from idols to himself. <reference osisRef="Isa.17.7-Isa.17.8">Isa. xvii. 7, 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">At that day shall a man look to his Maker.</hi> It may be read thus, <hi type="italic">for the Lord has an eye upon man, and upon all the tribes of Israel;</hi> he is King of nations as well as King of saints; he governs the world as well as the church, and therefore will punish the sins of other people as well as those of his own people. God is <hi type="italic">Judge of all,</hi> and therefore all must give account of themselves to him. When St. Paul was converted at Damascus, and preached there, and disputed with the Jews, then the word of the Lord might be said to rest there, and then <hi type="italic">the eyes of men,</hi> of other men besides <hi type="italic">the tribes of Israel,</hi> began to be <hi type="italic">towards the Lord;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Acts.9.22">Acts ix. 22</reference>. Hamath, a country which lay north of Damascus, and which we often read of, <hi type="italic">shall border thereby</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.2">v. 2</reference>); it joins to Syria, and shall share in the <hi type="italic">burden of the word of the Lord</hi> that rests upon Damascus. The Jews have a proverb, <hi type="italic">Woe to the wicked man, and woe to his neighbour,</hi> who is in danger of partaking in his sins and in his plagues. Woe to <hi type="italic">the land of Hadrach,</hi> and woe to <hi type="italic">Hamath that borders thereby.</hi> <div eID="gen20912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20913" type="x-p"/> II. Tyre and Zidon come next to be called to an account here, as in other prophecies, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.2-Zech.9.4">v. 2-4</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen20913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20914" type="x-p"/> 1. Tyrus flourishing, thinking herself very safe, and ready to set God's judgments, not only at a distance, but at defiance: for, (1.) She is <hi type="italic">very wise.</hi> It is spoken ironically; she thinks herself very wise, and able to outwit even the wisdom of God. It is granted that her king is a great politician, and that her statesmen are so, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.3">Ezek. xxviii. 3</reference>. But with all their wit and policy they shall not be able to evade the judgments of God when they come with commission; there is no <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> nor <hi type="italic">counsel against the Lord;</hi> nay, it is his honour to take the wise in their own craftiness. (2.) She is very strong, and well fortified both by nature and art: <hi type="italic">Tyrus did build herself a strong-hold,</hi> which she thought could never be brought down nor got over. (3.) She is very rich; and <hi type="italic">money is a defence;</hi> it is the sinews of war, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.12">Eccl. vii. 12</reference>. By her vast trade she has <hi type="italic">heaped up silver as the dust, and fine gold as the mire of the streets,</hi> that is, she has an abundance of them, heaps of silver as common as heaps of sand, <reference osisRef="Job.27.16">Job xxvii. 16</reference>. Solomon made silver to be in Jerusalem as the <hi type="italic">stones of the streets;</hi> but Tyre went further, and made <hi type="italic">fine gold</hi> to be as <hi type="italic">the mire of the streets.</hi> It were well if we could all learn so to look upon it, in comparison with the merchandise of wisdom and grace and the gains thereof. <div eID="gen20914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20915" type="x-p"/> 2. Tyrus falling, after all. Her wisdom, and wealth, and strength, shall not be able to secure her (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord will cast her out</hi> of that strong-hold wherein she has fortified herself, will <hi type="italic">make her poor</hi> (so some read it); there have been instances of those that have fallen from the height of plenty to the depth of poverty, and great riches have come to nothing. God will <hi type="italic">smite her power in the sea;</hi> her being surrounded by the water shall not secure her, but <hi type="italic">she shall be devoured with fire,</hi> and burnt down to the ground. Tyrus, being seated in the midst of the water, was, one would have thought, in danger of being some time or other overflowed or washed away by that; yet God chooses to destroy it by the contrary element. Sometimes he brings ruin upon his enemies by those means which they least suspect. Water enough was nigh at hand to quench the flames of Tyre, and yet by them she shall be devoured; for who can put out the fire which the breath of the Almighty blows up? <div eID="gen20915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20916" type="x-p"/> III. God next contends with the Philistines, with their great cities and great lords, that bordered southward upon Israel. <div eID="gen20916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20917" type="x-p"/> 1. They shall be alarmed and affrighted by the word of the Lord lighting and resting upon Damascus (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.5">v. 5</reference>); the disgraces of Israel had many a time been <hi type="italic">published in the streets of Ashkelon,</hi> and they had triumphed in them; but now <hi type="italic">Ashkelon shall see</hi> the ruin of her friends and allies, and shall <hi type="italic">fear; Gaza also shall see it, and be very sorrowful, and Ekron,</hi> concluding that their own turns come next, now that the cup of trembling goes round. What will become of their house when their neighbour's is on fire? They had looked upon Tyre and Zidon as a barrier to their country; but, when those strong cities were ruined, their <hi type="italic">expectations</hi> from them <hi type="italic">were ashamed,</hi> as our expectation from all creatures will be in the issue. <div eID="gen20917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20918" type="x-p"/> 2. They shall themselves be ruined and wasted. (1.) The government shall be dissolved: <hi type="italic">The king shall perish from Gaza,</hi> not only the present king shall be cut off, but there shall be no succession, no successor, (2.) The cities shall be dispeopled: <hi type="italic">Ashkelon shall not be inhabited;</hi> the rightful owners shall be expelled, either slain or carried into captivity. (3.) Foreigners shall take possession of their land and become masters of all its wealth (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">A bastard shall dwell in Ashdod;</hi> a spurious brood of strangers shall enter upon the inheritances of the natives, which they have no more right to than a bastard has to the estates of the legitimate children. And thus God will <hi type="italic">cut off the pride of the Philistines,</hi> all the strength and wealth which they prided themselves in, and which were the ground of their confidence in themselves and their contempt of the Israel of God. This prophecy of the destruction of the Philistines, and of Damascus, and Tyre, was accomplished, not long after this, by Alexander the Great, who ravaged all these countries with his victorious army, took the cities, and planted colonies in them, which Quintus Curtius gives a particular account of in the history of his conquests. And some think he is meant by the bastard that shall dwell in Ashdod, for his mother Olympia owned him begotten in adultery, but pretended it was by Jupiter. The Jews afterwards got ground of the Philistines, Syrians, and others of their neighbours, took some of their cities from them and possessed their countries, as appears by the histories of Josephus and the Maccabees, and this was foretold before, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.4">Zeph. ii. 4,</reference> and <reference osisRef="Obad.1.20">Obad. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen20918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20919" type="x-p"/> 3. Some among them shall be converted, and brought home to God, by his gospel and grace; so some understand <reference osisRef="Zech.9.7">v. 7</reference>, as a promise, (1.) That God would take away the sins of these nations—<hi type="italic">their blood</hi> and <hi type="italic">their abominations,</hi> their cruelties and their idolatries. God will part between them and these sins which they have rolled under their tongue as a sweet morsel, and are as loth to part with as men are to part with the meat out of their mouths, and which they hold fast between their teeth. Nothing is too hard for the grace of God to do. (2.) That he would accept of a remnant of them for his own: <hi type="italic">He that remains shall be for our God.</hi> God would preserve a remnant even of these nations, that should be the monuments of his mercy and grace and be set apart for him; and the disadvantages of their birth shall be no bar to their acceptance with God, but a Philistine shall be as acceptable to God, upon gospel-terms, as one of Judah, nay, as a governor, or chief one, in Judah, and a man of Ekron shall be as a Jebusite, or a man of Jerusalem, as a proselyted Jebusite, as Araunah the Jebusite, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.16">2 Sam. xxiv. 16</reference>. In Christ Jesus there is no distinction of nations, but all are one in him, all alike welcome to him. <div eID="gen20919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20920" type="x-p"/> IV. In all this God intends mercy for Israel, and it is in kindness to them that God will deal thus with the neighbouring nations, to avenge their quarrel for what is past and to secure them for the future. <div eID="gen20920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20921" type="x-p"/> 1. Thus some understand the <reference osisRef="Zech.9.7">seventh verse</reference>, as intimating, (1.) That thus God would deliver his people from their bloody adversaries, who hated them, and to whom they were an abomination, when they were just ready to devour them and make a prey of them: I will <hi type="italic">take away his blood</hi> (that is, the blood of Israel) out of the mouth of the Philistines and <hi type="italic">from between their teeth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.12">Amos iii. 12</reference>), when, in their hatred of them and enmity to them, they were greedily devouring them. (2.) That lie would thus give them victory and dominion over them: And <hi type="italic">he that remains</hi> (that is, the remnant of Israel) <hi type="italic">shall be for our God,</hi> shall be taken into his favour, shall own him and be owned by him, and <hi type="italic">he shall be as a governor in Judah;</hi> though the Jews have been long in servitude, they shall recover their ancient dignity, and be victorious, as David and other governors in Judah formerly were; and Ekron (that is, the Philistines) shall be as the Jebusites, and the rest of the devoted nations, who were brought into subjection under them. <div eID="gen20921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20922" type="x-p"/> 2. However, this is plainly the sense of <reference osisRef="Zech.9.8">v. 8</reference>, that God will take his people under his special protection, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> will weaken their neighbours, that it may not be in their power to do them a mischief: <hi type="italic">I will encamp about my house because of the army.</hi> Note, God's house lies in the midst of an enemy's country, and his church is as a lily among thorns; and therefore God's power and goodness are to be observed in the special preservation of it. The <hi type="italic">camp of the saints,</hi> being a little flock in comparison with the numerous armies of the powers of darkness that are set against it round about, would certainly be swallowed up if the angels of God did not encamp about it, as they did about Elisha, to deliver it, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.9">Rev. xx. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.7">Ps. xxxiv. 7</reference>. When the times are unusually perilous, when armies are marching and counter-marching, and all bearing ill-will to Zion, then Providence will as it were double its guards upon the church of God, <hi type="italic">because of him that passes by and because of him that returns,</hi> that whether he return a conqueror or conquered he may do it no harm. And, as none that pass by shall hurt them, so <hi type="italic">no oppressor shall pass through them any more;</hi> they shall have no enemy within themselves to rule them with rigour, and <hi type="italic">to make their lives bitter</hi> to them <hi type="italic">with sore bondage,</hi> as of old in Egypt. This was fulfilled when, for some time after the struggles of the Maccabees, Judea was a free and flourishing state, or perhaps when Alexander the Great, struck with an awe of Jaddus the high priest, favoured the Jews, and took them under his protection, at the same time when he wasted the neighbouring countries. And the reason given for all this is, "<hi type="italic">For now have I seen with my eyes,</hi> now have I carefully distinguished between my people and other people, with whom before they seemed to have their lot in common, and have made it to appear that I know those that are mine," This agrees with <reference osisRef="Ps.34.15">Ps. xxxiv. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous;</hi> now his eyes, which <hi type="italic">run to and fro through the earth,</hi> shall fix upon them, that he may show himself tender of them, and <hi type="italic">strong on their behalf,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 9</reference>.
entries.5f6584e804da5804a7dc3fd5c099037815c0ff92: <div eID="gen20922" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Predictions Relating to Messiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen20923" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he <hi type="italic">is</hi> just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass. <hi type="super">10</hi> And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off: and he shall speak peace unto the heathen: and his dominion <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> from sea <hi type="italic">even</hi> to sea, and from the river <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the ends of the earth. <hi type="super">11</hi> As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein <hi type="italic">is</hi> no water. <div eID="gen20923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20924" type="x-p"/> That here begins a prophecy of the Messiah and his kingdom is plain from the literal accomplishment of the <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">ninth verse</reference> in, and its express application to, Christ's riding in triumph into <hi type="italic">Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.5">Matt. xxi. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.15">John xii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen20924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20925" type="x-p"/> I. Here is notice given of the approach of the Messiah promised, as matter of great joy to the Old-Testament church: <hi type="italic">Behold, thy king cometh unto thee.</hi> Christ is a king, invested with regal powers and prerogatives, a sovereign prince, an absolute monarch, having all power both in heaven and on earth. He is Zion's king. God has <hi type="italic">set him upon his holy hill of Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>. In Zion his glory as a king shines; thence <hi type="italic">his law went forth,</hi> even the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord.</hi> In the gospel-church his spiritual kingdom is administered; it is by him that the ordinances of the church are instituted, and its officers commissioned; and it is taken under his protection; he fights the church's battles and secures its interests, as its king. "This King has been long in coming, but now, <hi type="italic">behold, he cometh;</hi> he is at the door. There are but a few ages more to run out, and he that shall come will come. He <hi type="italic">cometh unto thee;</hi> the Word will shortly be made flesh, and dwell within thy borders; he will <hi type="italic">come to his own.</hi> And therefore <hi type="italic">rejoice,</hi> rejoice <hi type="italic">greatly,</hi> and <hi type="italic">shout for joy;</hi> look upon it as <hi type="italic">good news,</hi> and be assured it is true; please thyself to think that he is coming, that he is on his way towards thee; and be ready to go forth to meet him with acclamations of joy, as one not able to conceal it, it is so great, nor ashamed to own it, it is so just; cry <hi type="italic">Hosanna</hi> to him." Christ's approaches ought to be the church's applauses. <div eID="gen20925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20926" type="x-p"/> II. Here is such a description of him as renders him very amiable in the eyes of all his loving subjects, and his coming to them very acceptable. 1. He is a righteous ruler; all his acts of government will be exactly according to the rules of equity, for <hi type="italic">he is just.</hi> 2. He is a powerful protector to all those that bear faith and true allegiance to him, for he <hi type="italic">has salvation;</hi> he has it in his power; he has it to bestow upon all his subjects. He is the <hi type="italic">God of salvation;</hi> treasures of salvation are in him. He is <hi type="italic">servatus</hi>—<hi type="italic">saving himself</hi> (so some read it), rising out of the grave by his own power and so qualifying himself to be our Saviour. (3.) He is a <hi type="italic">meek, humble, tender Father</hi> to all his subjects as his children; he is <hi type="italic">lowly;</hi> he is <hi type="italic">poor</hi> and <hi type="italic">afflicted</hi> (so the word signifies), so it denotes the meanness of his condition; having <hi type="italic">emptied himself,</hi> he was <hi type="italic">despised and rejected of men.</hi> But the evangelist translates it so as to express the temper of his spirit: he is <hi type="italic">meek,</hi> not taking state upon him, nor resenting injuries, but <hi type="italic">humbling himself</hi> from first to last, condescending to the mean, compassionate to the miserable; this was a bright and excellent character of him as a prophet (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Matt. xi. 29</reference>, <hi type="italic">Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart</hi>), and no less so <hi type="italic">as a king.</hi> It was a proof of this that, when he made his public entry into his own city (and it was the only passage of his life that had any thing in it magnificent in the eye of the world), he chose to ride, not upon a stately horse, or in a chariot, as great men used to ride, but <hi type="italic">upon an ass,</hi> a beast of service indeed, but a poor silly and contemptible one, low and slow, and in those days ridden only by the meaner sort of people; nor was it an ass fitted for use, but an <hi type="italic">ass's colt,</hi> a little foolish unmanageable thing, that would be more likely to disgrace his rider than be any credit to him; and that not his own neither, nor helped off, as sometimes a sorry horse is, by good furniture, for he had no saddle, no housings, no trappings, no equipage, but his disciples' clothes thrown upon the colt;' for he <hi type="italic">made himself of no reputation</hi> when he visited us in great humility. <div eID="gen20926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20927" type="x-p"/> III. His kingdom is here set forth in the glory of it. This king has, and will have, a kingdom, not of this world, but a spiritual kingdom, a <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven.</hi> 1. It shall not be set up and advanced by external force, by an arm of flesh or carnal weapons of warfare. No; he <hi type="italic">will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horses from Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">v. 10</reference>), for he shall have no occasion for them while he himself rides upon an ass. He will, in kindness to his people, cut off their horses and chariots, that they may not cut themselves off from God by putting that confidence in them which they should put in the power of God only. He will himself undertake their protection, will himself be <hi type="italic">a wall of fire about Jerusalem</hi> and give his angels charge concerning it (those <hi type="italic">chariots of fire and horses of fire</hi>), and then the chariots and horses they had in their service shall be discarded and cut off as altogether needless. 2. It shall be propagated and established by the preaching of the gospel, the <hi type="italic">speaking of peace to the heathen;</hi> for Christ <hi type="italic">came and preached peace to those that were afar off and to those that were nigh;</hi> and so established his kingdom by proclaiming <hi type="italic">on earth peace,</hi> and <hi type="italic">good-will towards men.</hi> 3. His kingdom, as far as it prevails in the minds of men and has the ascendant over them, will make them peaceable, and slay all enmities; it will cut off the battle-bow, and <hi type="italic">beat swords into plough-shares.</hi> It will not only command the peace, but will <hi type="italic">create the fruit of the lips, peace.</hi> 4. It shall extend itself to all parts of the world, in defiance of the opposition given to it. "The chariot and horse that come against Ephraim and Jerusalem, to oppose the progress of Zion's King, shall be cut off; his gospel shall be preached to the world, and be received among the heathen, so that <hi type="italic">his dominion shall be from sea to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth,</hi> as was foretold by David," <reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">Ps. lxxii. 8</reference>. The preachers of the gospel shall carry it from one country, one island, to another, till some of the remotest corners of the world are enlightened and reduced by it. <div eID="gen20927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20928" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is an account of the great benefit procured for mankind by the Messiah, which is redemption from extreme misery, typified by the deliverance of the Jews out of their captivity in Babylon (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">As for thee also</hi> (thee, O daughter of Jerusalem! or thee, O Messiah the Prince!) <hi type="italic">by the blood of thy covenant,</hi> by force and virtue of the covenant made with Abraham, sealed with the blood of circumcision, and the covenant made with Israel at Mount Sinai, sealed with the blood of sacrifices, in pursuance and performance of that covenant, <hi type="italic">I have</hi> now of late <hi type="italic">sent forth thy prisoners,</hi> thy captives out of Babylon, which was to them a most uncomfortable place, as <hi type="italic">a pit</hi> in which was <hi type="italic">no water.</hi>" It was part of the covenant that, if in the land of their captivity, they sought the Lord, he would be found of them, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.42 Lev.26.44 Lev.26.45">Lev. xxvi. 42, 44, 45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.30.4">Deut. xxx. 4</reference>. It was <hi type="italic">by the blood of that covenant,</hi> typifying the blood of Christ, in whom all God's covenants with man are yea and amen, that they were released out of captivity; and this was but a shadow of the great salvation wrought out by <hi type="italic">thy King, O daughter of Zion!</hi> Note, A sinful state is a state of bondage; it is a spiritual prison; it is a pit, or a dungeon, in which <hi type="italic">there is no water,</hi> no comfort at all to be had. We are all by nature prisoners in this pit; the <hi type="italic">scripture has concluded</hi> us all <hi type="italic">under sin,</hi> and bound us over to the justice of God. God is pleased to deal upon new terms with these prisoners, to enter into another covenant with them; the blood of Christ is the blood of that covenant, purchased it for us and all the benefits of it; by that blood of the covenant effectual provision is made for the sending forth of these prisoners upon easy and honourable terms, and proclamation made of <hi type="italic">liberty to the captives and the opening of the prison to those that were bound,</hi> like Cyrus's proclamation to the Jews in Babylon, which all those whose spirits God stirs up will come and take the benefit of.
entries.bf4c21dc3461368be6ba9a9753424bf418c68513: <div eID="gen20928" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Gospel Invitations; Promises of God's Favour to Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen20929" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope: even to day do I declare <hi type="italic">that</hi> I will render double unto thee; <hi type="super">13</hi> When I have bent Judah for me, filled the bow with Ephraim, and raised up thy sons, O Zion, against thy sons, O Greece, and made thee as the sword of a mighty man. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be seen over them, and his arrow shall go forth as the lightning: and the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> shall blow the trumpet, and shall go with whirlwinds of the south. <hi type="super">15</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts shall defend them; and they shall devour, and subdue with sling stones; and they shall drink, <hi type="italic">and</hi> make a noise as through wine; and they shall be filled like bowls, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as the corners of the altar. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people: for they <hi type="italic">shall be as</hi> the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land. <hi type="super">17</hi> For how great <hi type="italic">is</hi> his goodness, and how great <hi type="italic">is</hi> his beauty! corn shall make the young men cheerful, and new wine the maids. <div eID="gen20929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20930" type="x-p"/> The prophet, having taught those that had returned out of captivity to attribute their deliverance to the <hi type="italic">blood of the covenant</hi> and to the promise of the Messiah (for they were so wonderfully helped because that blessing was in them, was yet in the womb of their nation), now comes to encourage them with the prospect of a joyful and happy settlement, and of glorious times before them; and such a happiness they did enjoy, in a great measure, for some time; but these promises have their full accomplishment in the spiritual blessings of the gospel which we enjoy by Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen20930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20931" type="x-p"/> I. They are invited to look unto Christ, and flee unto him as their city of refuge (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Turn you to the strong-hold, you prisoners of hope.</hi> The Jews that had returned out of captivity into their own land were yet, in effect, but <hi type="italic">prisoners (We are servants this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.36">Neh. ix. 36</reference>), yet <hi type="italic">prisoners of hope,</hi> or <hi type="italic">expectation,</hi> for God had given them a <hi type="italic">little reviving in their bondage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezra ix. 8, 9</reference>. Those that yet continued in Babylon, detained by their affairs there, yet lived in hope some time or other to see their own land again. Now both these are directed to turn their eyes upon the Messiah, set before them in the promise as their strong-hold, to shelter themselves in him, and stay themselves upon him, for the perfecting of the mercy which by his grace, and for his sake, was so gloriously begun. <hi type="italic">Look unto him, and be you saved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.22">Isa. xlv. 22</reference>. The promise of the Messiah was the strong-hold of the faithful long before his coming; they saw his day at a distance and were glad, and the believing expectation of the <hi type="italic">redemption in Jerusalem</hi> was long the support and <hi type="italic">consolation of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.25">Luke ii. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.38">38</reference>. They, in their dangers and distresses, were ready to turn towards this and the other creature for relief; but the prophets directed them still to turn to Christ, and to comfort themselves with the joy of their king coming to them with salvation. But, as their deliverance was typical of our redemption by Christ (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.11">v. 11</reference>), so this invitation to the strong-hold speaks the language of the gospel-call. Sinners are prisoners, but they are prisoners of hope; their case is sad, but it is not desperate; yet now there is hope in Israel concerning them. Christ is a strong-hold for them, a strong tower, in whom they may be safe and quiet from the fear of the wrath of God, the curse of the law, and the assaults of their spiritual enemies. To him they must turn by a lively faith; to him they must flee, and trust in his name. <div eID="gen20931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20932" type="x-p"/> II. They are assured of God's favour to them: "<hi type="italic">Even to day do I declare,</hi> when things are at the worst, and you think your case deplorable to the last degree, yet I solemnly promise that <hi type="italic">I will render double unto thee,</hi> to thee, O Jerusalem! to every one of you prisoners of hope. I will give you comforts double to the sorrows you have experienced, or blessings double to what I ever bestowed upon your fathers, when their condition was at the best; the glory of your latter state, as well as of your latter house, shall be greater, shall be twice as great as that of your former." And so it was no otherwise than by the coming of the Messiah, the preaching of his gospel, and the setting up of his kingdom; these spiritual blessings in heavenly things were double to what they had ever enjoyed in their most prosperous state. As a pledge of this, in the fulness of time God here promises to the Jews victory, plenty, and joy, in their own land, which yet should be but a type and shadow of more glorious victories, riches, and joys, in the kingdom of Christ. <div eID="gen20932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20933" type="x-p"/> 1. They shall triumph over their enemies. The Jews, after their return, were surrounded with enemies on all sides. They were <hi type="italic">as a speckled bird;</hi> all the birds of the field were against them. Their land lay between the two potent kingdoms of Syria and Egypt, branches of the Grecian monarchy, and what frequent dangers they should be in between them was foretold, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.1-Dan.11.45">Dan. xi</reference>. But it is here promised that out of them all the Lord would deliver them; and this promise had its primary accomplishment in the times of the Maccabees, when the Jews made head against their enemies, kept their head above water, and, after many struggles and difficulties, came to be head over them. It is promised, (1.) That they shall be instruments in God's hand for the defeating and baffling of their persecutors: "I <hi type="italic">have bent Judah for me,</hi> as my bow of steel; that <hi type="italic">bow I have filled with Ephraim</hi> as my arrows, have drawn it up to its full bent, till the arrow be at the head;" for some think that this is signified by the phrase of <hi type="italic">filling the bow.</hi> The expressions here are very fine, and the figures lively. Judah had been <hi type="italic">taught the use of the bow</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.18">2 Sam. i. 18</reference>), and Ephraim had been famous for it, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.9">Ps. lxxviii. 9</reference>. But let them not think that they gain their successes by their own bow, for they themselves are no more than God's bow and his arrows, tools in his hands, which he makes use of and manages as he pleases, which he holds as his bow and directs to the mark as his arrows. The best and bravest of men are but what God makes them, and do no more service than he enables them to do. The preachers of the gospel were the bow in Christ's hand, with which he went forth, he went on, <hi type="italic">conquering and to conquer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev. vi. 2</reference>. The following words explain this: <hi type="italic">I have raised up</hi> and animated <hi type="italic">thy sons, O Zion! against thy sons, O Greece!</hi> This was fulfilled when <hi type="italic">against Antiochus,</hi> one of the kings of the Grecian monarchy, the people that knew their God were <hi type="italic">strong</hi> and <hi type="italic">did exploits,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.32">Dan. xi. 32</reference>. And they in the hand of an almighty God were made <hi type="italic">as the sword of a mighty man,</hi> which none can stand before. Wicked men are said to be God's sword (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Ps. xvii. 13</reference>), and sometimes good men are made so; for he employs both as he pleases. (2.) That God will be captain, and commander-in-chief, over them, in every expedition and engagement (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord shall be seen over them;</hi> he shall make it appear that he presides in their affairs, and that in all their motions they are under his direction, as apparently, though not as sensibly, as he was <hi type="italic">seen over Israel</hi> in the pillar of cloud and fire when he led them through the wilderness. [1.] Is their army to be raised, or mustered, and brought into the field? <hi type="italic">The Lord shall blow the trumpet,</hi> to gather the forces together, to proclaim the war, to sound the alarm, and to give directions which way to march, which way to move; for, if God blow the trumpet, it shall not give an uncertain sound, nor a feeble ineffectual one. [2.] Is the army taking the field, and entering upon action? Whatever enterprise the campaign is opened with, God shall go forth at the head of their forces, <hi type="italic">with whirlwinds of the south,</hi> which were of incredible swiftness and fierceness; and before these whirlwinds thy sons, O Greece! shall be as chaff. [3.] Is the army actually engaged? God's <hi type="italic">arrows shall go forth as lightning,</hi> so strongly, so suddenly, so irresistibly; his <hi type="italic">lightnings</hi> shall go forth <hi type="italic">as arrows</hi> and <hi type="italic">scattered them,</hi> that is, he <hi type="italic">shot out his lightnings and discomfited them.</hi> This alludes to that which God had done for Israel of old when he brought them out of Egypt, and into Canaan, and had its accomplishment partly in the wonderful successes which the Jews had against their neighbours that attacked them in the time of the Maccabees, by the special appearances of the divine Providence for them, and perfectly in the glorious victories gained by the cross of Christ and the preaching of the cross over Satan and all the powers of darkness, whereby we are made more than conquerors. [4.] Are they in danger of being overpowered by the enemy? <hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts shall defend them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.15">v. 15</reference>); <hi type="italic">The Lord their God shall save them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.16">v. 16</reference>); so that their enemies shall not prevail over them, nor prey upon them. God shall be unto them for defence as well as offence, <hi type="italic">the shield of their help</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">the sword of their excellency,</hi> and this as <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> who has power to defend them, and as <hi type="italic">their God,</hi> who is engaged by promise to defend them, and by the property he has in them. He shall save them in <hi type="italic">that day,</hi> that critical dangerous day, <hi type="italic">as the flock of his people,</hi> with the same care and tenderness that the shepherd protects his sheep with. Those are safe whom God saves. [5.] Did their enemies hope to swallow them up? It shall be turned upon them, and they shall <hi type="italic">devour</hi> their enemies, and shall <hi type="italic">subdue with sling-stones,</hi> for want of better weapons, those that come forth against them. The <hi type="italic">stones of the brook,</hi> when God pleases, shall do as great execution as the best train of artillery; for the <hi type="italic">stars in their courses</hi> shall fight on the same side. Goliath was subdued with a sling-stone. Having subdued, they shall <hi type="italic">devour, shall drink</hi> the blood of their enemies, as it were, and, as conquerors are wont to do, they shall <hi type="italic">make a noise as through wine.</hi> It is usual for conquerors with loud huzzas and acclamations to glory in their victories and proclaim them. We read of those that <hi type="italic">shout for mastery,</hi> and of the <hi type="italic">shout of a king</hi> among God's people. They shall be filled with blood and spoil, as the bowls and basins of the temple, or the <hi type="italic">corners of the altar,</hi> were wont to be filled with the blood of the sacrifices; for their enemies shall fall as victims to divine justice. <div eID="gen20933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20934" type="x-p"/> 2. They shall triumph in their God. They shall take the comfort and give God the glory of their successes. So some read <reference osisRef="Zech.9.15">v. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">They shall eat</hi> (that is, they shall quietly enjoy) what they have got; God will give them power to eat it <hi type="italic">after they have subdued the sling-stones</hi> (that is, their enemies that slung stones at them), and <hi type="italic">they shall drink and make a noise,</hi> a joyful noise, before the Lord their maker and protector, <hi type="italic">as through wine,</hi> as men are merry at a banquet of wine. <hi type="italic">Being not drunk with wine, wherein is excess,</hi> but <hi type="italic">filled with the Spirit,</hi> they shall <hi type="italic">speak</hi> to themselves and one another <hi type="italic">in psalms, and hymns, and spiritual songs,</hi> as those that are drunk do with vain and foolish songs, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.18-Eph.5.19">Eph. v. 18, 19</reference>. And, in the fulness of their joy, they shall offer abundance of sacrifices to the honour of God, so that <hi type="italic">they shall fill both the bowls and the corners of the altar</hi> with the fat and blood of their sacrifices. And, when they thus triumph in their successes, their joy shall terminate in God as their God, the God of their salvation. They shall triumph, (1.) In the love he has for them, and the relation wherein they stand to him, that they are <hi type="italic">the flock of his people</hi> and he is their Shepherd, and that they are to him <hi type="italic">as the stones of a crown,</hi> which are very precious and of great value, and which are kept under a strong guard. Never was any king so pleased with the jewels of his crown as God is, and will be, with his people, who are near and dear unto him, and in whom he glories. They are a <hi type="italic">crown of glory</hi> and a <hi type="italic">royal diadem</hi> in his hand, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.2-Isa.62.3">Isa. lxii. 2, 3</reference>. And <hi type="italic">they shall be mine, saith the Lord, in that day when I make up my jewels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.17">Mal. iii. 17</reference>. And <hi type="italic">they shall be lifted up as an ensign upon his land,</hi> as the royal standard is displayed in token of triumph and joy. God's people are his glory; so he is pleased to make them, so he is pleased to reckon them. He sets them up as a banner upon his own land, waging war against those who hate him, to whom it is a flag of defiance, while it is a centre of unity to all that love him, to all the children of God, that are scattered abroad, who are invited to come and enlist themselves under this banner, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Isa. xi. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">12</reference>. (2.) In the provision he makes for them, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.15">v. 15</reference>. This is the matter of their triumph (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">For how great is his goodness and how great is his beauty!</hi> This is the substance, this the burden, of the songs wherewith they shall <hi type="italic">make a noise</hi> before the Lord. We are here taught, [1.] To admire and praise the amiableness of God's being: <hi type="italic">How great is his beauty!</hi> All the perfections of God's nature conspire to make him infinitely lovely in the eyes of all that know him. They are to him as the <hi type="italic">stones of a crown;</hi> but what is he to them? Our business in the temple is to <hi type="italic">behold the beauty of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>), and <hi type="italic">how great is that beauty!</hi> How far does it transcend all other beauties, particularly the <hi type="italic">beauty of his holiness.</hi> This may refer to the Messiah, to Zion's <hi type="italic">King</hi> that <hi type="italic">cometh.</hi> See <hi type="italic">that king in his beauty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.17">Isa. xxxiii. 17</reference>), who is <hi type="italic">fairer than the children of men,</hi> the <hi type="italic">fairest of ten thousand,</hi> and <hi type="italic">altogether lovely.</hi> Though, in the eye of the world, he had no form or comeliness, in the eye of faith how great is his beauty! [2.] To admire and give thanks for the gifts of God's favour and grace, his bounty as well as his beauty; for <hi type="italic">how great is his goodness!</hi> How rich in mercy is he! How deep, how full, are its springs! How various, how plenteous, how precious, are its streams! What a great deal of good does God do! How rich in mercy is he! Here is an instance of his goodness to his people: <hi type="italic">Corn shall make the young men cheerful and new wine the maids;</hi> that is, God will bless his people with an abundance of the fruits of the earth. Whereas they had been afflicted with scarcity to such a degree that the <hi type="italic">young men</hi> and the <hi type="italic">maidens</hi> were ready to swoon and faint away for hunger and thirst (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.12 Lam.2.21 Lam.4.7-Lam.4.8">Lam. ii. 12, 21; iv. 7, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.10">v. 10</reference>), now they shall have bread enough and to spare, not water only, but <hi type="italic">wine, new wine,</hi> which shall make the young people grow and be cheerful, and (which some have observed to be the effect of plenty and the cheapness of corn) the poor will be encouraged to marry, and re-people the land, when they shall have wherewithal to maintain their families. Note, What good gifts God bestows upon us we must serve him cheerfully with, and must race the streams up to the fountain, and, when we are refreshed with corn and wine, must say, <hi type="italic">How great is his goodness!</hi>  <chapter eID="Zech.9"/> <div eID="gen20934" type="x-p"/>

entries.ad32665c564889b45ea8391b0af99789772ad17e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13123"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.9.1-Zech.9.17">Zec 9:1-17</reference>. Ninth to Fourteenth Chapters Are Prophetical.</title> <div sID="gen24685" type="x-p"/> Written long after the previous portions of the book, whence arise the various features which have been made grounds for attacking their authenticity, notwithstanding the testimony of the Septuagint and of the compilers of the Jewish canon in their favor. See Introduction.<div eID="gen24685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24686" type="x-p"/> Alexander's Conquests in Syria (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.1-Zech.9.8">Zec 9:1-8</reference>). God's People Safe because Her King Cometh Lowly, but a Saviour (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.9-Zech.9.10">Zec 9:9-10</reference>). The Maccabean Deliverance a Type Thereof (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.11-Zech.9.17">Zec 9:11-17</reference>).<div eID="gen24686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13123"/><hi type="bold">1. in ... Hadrach--</hi>rather, concerning or against Hadrach (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.21.13">Is 21:13</reference>). "Burden" means a prophecy BURDENED with wrath against the guilty. Maurer, not so well, explains it, What is taken up and uttered, the utterance, a solemn declaration.<div eID="gen24687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hadrach--</hi>a part of Syria, near Damascus. As the name is not mentioned in ancient histories, it probably was the less-used name of a region having two names ("Hadrach" and "Bikathaven," <reference osisRef="Amos.1.5">Am 1:5</reference>, Margin); hence it passed into oblivion. An ancient Rabbi Jose is, however, stated to have expressly mentioned it. An Arab, Jos. Abassi, in 1768 also declared to Michaelis that there was then a town of that name, and that it was capital of the region Hadrach. The name means "enclosed" in Syrian, that is, the west interior part of Syria, enclosed by hills, the Coelo-Syria of Strabo [Maurer]. Jerome considers Hadrach to be the metropolis of Coelo-Syria, as Damascus was of the region about that city. Hengstenberg regards Hadrach as a symbolical name of Persia, which Zechariah avoids designating by its proper name so as not to offend the government under which he lived. But the context seems to refer to the Syrian region. Gesenius thinks that the name is that of a Syrian king, which might more easily pass into oblivion than that of a region. Compare the similar "land of Sihon," <reference osisRef="Neh.9.22">Ne 9:22</reference>.<div eID="gen24688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Damascus ... rest thereof--</hi>that is, the place on which the "burden" of the Lord's wrath shall rest. It shall permanently settle on it until Syria is utterly prostrate. Fulfilled under Alexander the Great, who overcame Syria [Curtius, Books 3 and 4].<div eID="gen24689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes of man, as of all ... Israel ... toward the Lord--</hi>The eyes of men in general, and of all Israel in particular, through consternation at the victorious progress of Alexander, shall be directed to Jehovah. The Jews, when threatened by him because of Jaddua the high priest's refusal to swear fealty to him, prayed earnestly to the Lord, and so were delivered (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.12">2Ch 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.23.2">Psa 23:2</reference>). Typical of the effect of God's judgments hereafter on all men, and especially on the Jews in turning them to Him. Maurer, Pembellus and others, less probably translate, "The eyes of the Lord are upon man, as they are upon all Israel," namely, to punish the ungodly and to protect His people. He, who has chastised His people, will not fail to punish men for their sins severely. The "all," I think, implies that whereas men's attention generally (whence "man" is the expression) was directed to Jehovah's judgments, all Israel especially looks to Him. <div eID="gen24690" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4a788147f2030c1c16cba49eceaa106a4535314: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13124"/><div sID="gen24691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13124"/><hi type="bold">2. Hamath--</hi>a Syrian kingdom with a capital of the same name, north of Damascus.<div eID="gen24691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall border thereby--</hi>shall be joined to Damascus in treatment, as it is in position; shall share in the burden of wrath of which Damascus is the resting-place. Maurer understands "which"; "Hamath, which borders on Damascus, also shall be the resting-place of Jehovah's wrath" (the latter words being supplied from <reference osisRef="Zech.9.1">Zec 9:1</reference>). Riblah, the scene of the Jews' sufferings from their foe, was there: it therefore shall suffer (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.33">2Ki 23:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.6">25:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.20">7, 20</reference>, 21).<div eID="gen24692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tyrus ... Zidon--</hi>lying in the conqueror's way on his march along the Mediterranean to Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1-Isa.23.18">Is 23:1-18</reference>). Zidon, the older city, surrendered, and Abdolonymus was made its viceroy.<div eID="gen24693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">very wise--</hi>in her own eyes. Referring to Tyre: <reference osisRef="Zech.9.3">Zec 9:3</reference> shows wherein her wisdom consisted, namely, in building a stronghold, and heaping up gold and silver (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.3">Eze 38:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">5, 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.17">17</reference>). On Alexander's expressing his wish to sacrifice in Hercules' temple in New Tyre on the island, she showed her wisdom in sending a golden crown, and replying that the true and ancient temple of Hercules was at Old Tyre on the mainland. With all her wisdom she cannot avert her doom. <div eID="gen24694" type="x-p"/>
entries.36d1cb420e2342d1f680e2c47d674cd427d69273: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13125"/><div sID="gen24695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13125"/>3. The heathen historian, Diodorus Siculus [17.40], confirms this. "Tyre had the greatest confidence owing to her insular position and fortifications, and the abundant stores she had prepared." New Tyre was on an island seven hundred paces from the shore. As Isaiah's and Ezekiel's (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.1-Ezek.27.36">Eze 27:1-36</reference>) prophecies were directed against Old Tyre on the mainland and were fulfilled by Nebuchadnezzar, so Zechariah's are against New Tyre, which was made seemingly impregnable by a double wall one hundred fifty feet high, as well as the sea on all sides. <div eID="gen24695" type="x-p"/>
entries.63286cb7f93819bc72965186adfeca2a082e2a58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13126"/><div sID="gen24696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13126"/>4. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.4">Eze 26:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.27">27:27</reference>).<div eID="gen24696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24697" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast her out--</hi>Hebrew, "dispossess her," that is, will cast her inhabitants into exile [Grotius]. Alexander, though without a navy, by incredible labor constructed a mole of the ruins of Old Tyre (fulfilling <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.4-Ezek.26.12">Eze 26:4-12</reference>, &c., by "scraping her dust from her," and "laying her stones, timber, and dust in the midst of the water"), from the shore to the island, and, after a seven months' siege, took the city by storm, slew with the sword about eight thousand, enslaved thirteen thousand, crucified two thousand, and set the city on "fire," as here foretold [Curtius, Book 4].<div eID="gen24697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smite her power in the sea--</hi>situated though she be in the sea, and so seeming impregnable (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference>, "I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the sea"). "Her power" includes not only her fortifications, but her fleet, all of which Alexander sank in the sea before her very walls [Curtius, Book 4]. <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.17">Eze 26:17</reference> corresponds, "How art thou destroyed which wast strong in the sea!" <div eID="gen24698" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e8e2d3079024d2f7709f256a906ff750e6c61b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13127"/><div sID="gen24699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13127"/><hi type="bold">5. Ashkelon, &c.--</hi>Gath alone is omitted, perhaps as being somewhat inland, and so out of the route of the advancing conqueror.<div eID="gen24699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ekron ... expectation ... ashamed--</hi>Ekron, the farthest north of the Philistine cities, had expected Tyre would withstand Alexander, and so check his progress southward through Philistia to Egypt. This hope being confounded ("put to shame"), Ekron shall "fear."<div eID="gen24700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king shall perish from Gaza--</hi>Its government shall be overthrown. In literal fulfilment of this prophecy, after a two month's siege, Gaza was taken by Alexander, ten thousand of its inhabitants slain, and the rest sold as slaves. Betis the satrap, or petty "king," was bound to a chariot by thongs thrust through the soles of his feet, and dragged round the city. <div eID="gen24701" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c3acc75217cea67f338f976b2a0287aadd57699: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13128"/><div sID="gen24702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13128"/><hi type="bold">6. bastard--</hi>not the rightful heir; vile and low men, such as are bastards (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.2">De 23:2</reference>) [Grotius]. An alien; so the Septuagint; implying the desolation of the region wherein men shall not settle, but sojourn in only as aliens passing through [Calvin]. <div eID="gen24702" type="x-p"/>
entries.58cc0a283d769e1f135ac423a52cccf7c9ad9d66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13129"/><div sID="gen24703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13129"/><hi type="bold">7. take ... his blood out of ... mouth--</hi>Blood was forbidden as food (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Ge 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.7.26">Le 7:26</reference>).<div eID="gen24703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abominations--</hi>things sacrificed to idols and then partaken of by the worshippers (<reference osisRef="Num.25.2">Nu 25:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.29">Ac 15:29</reference>). The sense is, "I will cause the Philistines to cease from the worship of idols."<div eID="gen24704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even he shall be for our God--</hi>"even he," like Hamath, Damascus, Tyre, &c., which, these words imply, shall also be converted to God (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.3">Is 56:3</reference>, "son of the stranger joined himself to the Lord") [Rosenmuller]. The "even," however, may mean, Besides the Hebrews, "even" the Philistine shall worship Jehovah (so <reference osisRef="Isa.56.8">Is 56:8</reference>) [Maurer].<div eID="gen24705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall be as a governor in Judah--</hi>On the conversion of the Philistine prince, he shall have the same dignity "in Judah as a governor"; there shall be no distinction [Henderson]. The Philistine princes with their respective states shall equally belong to the Jews' communion, as if they were among the "governors" of states "in Judah" [Maurer].<div eID="gen24706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ekron as a Jebusite--</hi>The Jebusites, the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, who, when subjugated by David, were incorporated with the Jews (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.16">2Sa 24:16</reference>, &c.), and enjoyed their privileges: but in a subordinate position civilly (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.20">1Ki 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.21">21</reference>). The Jebusites' condition under Solomon being that of bond-servants and tributaries, Calvin explains the verse differently: "I will rescue the Jew from the teeth of the Philistine foe (image from wild beasts rending their prey with their teeth), who would have devoured him, as he would devour blood or flesh of his abominable sacrifices to idols: and even he, the seemingly ignoble remnant of the Jews, shall be sacred to our God (consecrated by His favor); and though so long bereft of dignity, I will make them to be as governors ruling others, and Ekron shall be a tributary bond-servant as the Jebusite? Thus the antithesis is between the Jew that remaineth (the elect remnant) and the Ekronite. <div eID="gen24707" type="x-p"/>
entries.a088b807d41b49c1b4863f4b00ddd16b9c5c3cc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13130"/><div sID="gen24708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13130"/><hi type="bold">8. encamp about--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.34.7">Psa 34:7</reference>).<div eID="gen24708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine house--</hi>namely, the Jewish people (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.7">Zec 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">Ho 8:1</reference>) [Maurer]. Or, the temple: reassuring the Jews engaged in building, who might otherwise fear their work would be undone by the conqueror [Moore]. The Jews were, in agreement with this prophecy, uninjured by Alexander, though he punished the Samaritans. Typical of their final deliverance from every foe.<div eID="gen24709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24710" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passeth by ... returneth--</hi>Alexander, when advancing against Jerusalem, was arrested by a dream, so that neither in "passing by" to Egypt, nor in "returning," did he injure the Jews, but conferred on them great privileges.<div eID="gen24710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no oppressor ... pass through ... any more--</hi>The prophet passes from the immediate future to the final deliverance to come (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.18">Is 60:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.24">Eze 28:24</reference>).<div eID="gen24711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seen with mine eyes--</hi>namely, how Jerusalem has been oppressed by her foes [Rosenmuller] (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.7">Ex 3:7</reference>; 2:25). God is said now to have seen, because He now begins to bring the foe to judgment, and manifests to the world His sense of His people's wrongs. <div eID="gen24712" type="x-p"/>
entries.9509ff1d0bfc33feb678a35d4abba7121dfbb8e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13131"/><div sID="gen24713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13131"/>9. From the coming of the Grecian conqueror, Zechariah makes a sudden transition, by the prophetical law of suggestion, to the coming of King Messiah, a very different character.<div eID="gen24713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughter of Zion--</hi>The theocratic people is called to "rejoice" at the coming of her King (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.11">Psa 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen24714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto thee--</hi>He comes not for His own gain or pleasure, as earthly kings come, but for the sake of His Church: especially for the Jews' sake, at His second coming (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>).<div eID="gen24715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24716" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is just--</hi>righteous: an attribute constantly given to Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">Is 45:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">53:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">6</reference>) in connection with salvation. He does not merely pardon by conniving at sin, but He justifies by becoming the Lord our righteousness fulfiller, so that not merely mercy, but justice, requires the justification of the sinner who by faith becomes one with Christ. God's justice is not set aside by the sinner's salvation, but is magnified and made honorable by it (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.21">21</reference>). His future reign "in righteousness," also, is especially referred to (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Is 32:1</reference>).<div eID="gen24716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having salvation--</hi>not passively, as some interpret it, "saved," which the context, referring to a "king" coming to reign, forbids; also the old versions, the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate, give Saviour. The Hebrew is reflexive in sense, "showing Himself a Saviour; ... having salvation in Himself" for us. Endowed with a salvation which He bestows as a king. Compare Margin, "saving Himself." Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Mt 1:21</reference>, in the Greek, "Himself shall save His people"; that is, not by any other, but by Himself shall He save [Pearson On the Creed]. His "having salvation" for others manifested that He had in Himself that righteousness which was indispensable for the justification of the unrighteous (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1Jo 2:1</reference>). This contrasts beautifully with the haughty Grecian conqueror who came to destroy, whereas Messiah came to save. Still, Messiah shall come to take "just" vengeance on His foes, previous to His reign of peace (Mal 4:1, 2).<div eID="gen24717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lowly--</hi>mild, gentle: corresponding to His "riding on an ass" (not a despised animal, as with us; nor a badge of humiliation, for princes in the East rode on asses, as well as low persons, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.10">Jud 5:10</reference>), that is, coming as "Prince of peace" (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">Zec 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>); the "horse," on the contrary is the emblem of war, and shall therefore be "cut off." Perhaps the Hebrew includes both the "lowliness" of His outward state (which applies to His first coming) and His "meekness" of disposition, as <reference osisRef="Matt.21.5">Mt 21:5</reference> quotes it (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>), which applies to both His comings. Both adapt Him for loving sympathy with us men; and at the same time are the ground of His coming manifested exaltation (<reference osisRef="John.5.27">Joh 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.7-Phil.2.9">Php 2:7-9</reference>).<div eID="gen24718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">colt--</hi>untamed, "whereon yet never man sat" (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.30">Lu 19:30</reference>). The symbol of a triumphant conqueror and judge (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.10">Jud 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.10.4">10:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.12.14">12:14</reference>).<div eID="gen24719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24720" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foal of an ass--</hi>literally, "asses": in Hebrew idiom, the indefinite plural for singular (so <reference osisRef="Gen.8.4">Ge 8:4</reference>, "mountains of Ararat," for one of the mountains). The dam accompanied the colt (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.2">Mt 21:2</reference>). The entry of Jesus into Jerusalem at His first coming is a pledge of the full accomplishment of this prophecy at His second coming. It shall be "the day of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.24">Psa 118:24</reference>), as that first Palm Sunday was. The Jews shall then universally (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.26">Psa 118:26</reference>) say, what some of them said then, "Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord" (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.21.9">Mt 21:9</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Matt.23.39">Mt 23:39</reference>); also "Hosanna," or "Save now, I beseech thee." "Palms," the emblem of triumph, shall then also be in the hands of His people (compare <reference osisRef="John.12.13">Joh 12:13</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Re 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.10">10</reference>). Then also, as on His former entry, shall be the feast of tabernacles (at which they used to draw water from Siloam, quoting <reference osisRef="Isa.12.3">Is 12:3</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.118.15">Psa 118:15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>. <div eID="gen24720" type="x-p"/>
entries.072d5b9d171e76d8268d34d92db1c90c27a34ddc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13132"/><div sID="gen24721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13132"/>10. (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Is 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.10">Mi 5:10</reference>).<div eID="gen24721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ephraim ... Jerusalem--</hi>the ten tribes, and Judah and Benjamin; both alike to be restored hereafter.<div eID="gen24722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speak peace--</hi>command it authoritatively.<div eID="gen24723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dominion ... from sea ... river ... ends of ... earth--</hi>fulfilling <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Ge 15:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.31">Ex 23:31</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">Psa 72:8</reference>. "Sea ... sea," are the Red Sea and Mediterranean. The "river" is the Euphrates. Jerusalem and the Holy Land, extended to the limits promised to Abraham, are to be the center of His future dominion; whence it will extend to the remotest parts of the earth. <div eID="gen24724" type="x-p"/>
entries.f59c821ada7e1caebe0b3a46bba3bcfdab2932bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13133"/><div sID="gen24725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13133"/><hi type="bold">11. As for thee also--</hi>that is, the daughter of Zion," or "Jerusalem" (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>): the theocracy. The "thee also," in contradistinction to Messiah spoken of in <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">Zec 9:10</reference>, implies that besides cutting off the battle-bow and extending Messiah's "dominion to the ends of the earth," God would also deliver for her her exiled people from their foreign captivity.<div eID="gen24725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the blood of thy covenant--</hi>that is, according to the covenant vouchsafed to thee on Sinai, and ratified by the blood of sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.8">Ex 24:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.18-Heb.9.20">He 9:18-20</reference>).<div eID="gen24726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pit wherein ... no water--</hi>Dungeons were often pits without water, miry at the bottom, such as Jeremiah sank in when confined (<reference osisRef="Gen.37.24">Ge 37:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">Jr 38:6</reference>). An image of the misery of the Jewish exiles in Egypt, Greece, &c., under the successors of Alexander, especially under Antiochus Epiphanes, who robbed and profaned the temple, slew thousands, and enslaved more. God delivered them by the Maccabees. A type of the future deliverance from their last great persecutor hereafter (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.14">Is 51:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.1">60:1</reference>). <div eID="gen24727" type="x-p"/>
entries.4baea079d9770c1b2587792061a9a44af422ab1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13134"/><div sID="gen24728" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13134"/><hi type="bold">12. stronghold--</hi>in contrast to the "pit" (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.11">Zec 9:11</reference>); literally, "a place cut off from access." Maurer thinks, "a height" (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.33">Psa 18:33</reference>). An image for the security which the returning Jews shall have in Messiah (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.8">Zec 9:8</reference>) encamped about His people (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.1">Psa 46:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.46.5">5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.49.9">Is 49:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Pr 18:10</reference>).<div eID="gen24728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prisoners of hope--</hi>that is, who in spite of afflictions (<reference osisRef="Job.13.15">Job 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Psa 42:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.11">11</reference>) maintain hope in the covenant-keeping God; in contrast to unbelievers, who say, "There is no hope" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jr 2:25</reference>; 18:12). Especially those Jews who believe God's word to Israel (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.17">Jr 31:17</reference>), "there is hope in the end, that thy children shall come again to their own border," and do not say, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.11">Eze 37:11</reference>, "Our hope is lost." Primarily, the Jews of Zechariah's time are encouraged not to be dispirited in building by their trials; secondarily, the Jews before the coming restoration are encouraged to look to Messiah for deliverance from their last oppressors.<div eID="gen24729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even to-day--</hi>when your circumstances seem so unpromising; in contrast with the "day of the Lord," when Zion's King shall come to her deliverance (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>).<div eID="gen24730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will render double--</hi>Great as has been thy adversity, thy prosperity shall be doubly greater (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Is 61:7</reference>). <div eID="gen24731" type="x-p"/>
entries.aabe2f237cf14580aad3a99a508bb6237dc8613e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13135"/><div sID="gen24732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13135"/><hi type="bold">13. bent Judah--</hi>made Judah as it were My bow, and "filled" it "with Ephraim," as My arrow, wherewith to overcome the successor of the Grecian Alexander, Antiochus Epiphanes (compare Notes, see on <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.32">Da 11:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1</reference> Maccabees 1:62; 2:41-43), the oppressor of Judah. Having spoken (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.1-Zech.9.8">Zec 9:1-8</reference>) of Alexander's victories, after the parenthesis (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">10</reference>) as to Messiah the infinitely greater King coming, he passes to the victories which God would enable Judah to gain over Alexander's successor, after his temporary oppression of them.<div eID="gen24732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">O Zion ... O Greece--</hi>God on one hand addresses Zion, on the other Greece, showing that He rules all people. <div eID="gen24733" type="x-p"/>
entries.99e2cd672e62480d0c09d82e4e6a04f40f4fc2cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13136"/><div sID="gen24734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13136"/>14. Another image: "Jehovah shall be seen (conspicuously manifesting His power) over them" (that is, in behalf of the Jews and against their foes), as formerly He appeared in a cloud over the Israelites against the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.19">Ex 14:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen24734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his arrow ... as ... lightning--</hi>flashing forth instantaneous destruction to the foe (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.14">Psa 18:14</reference>).<div eID="gen24735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24736" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blow ... trumpet--</hi>to summon and incite His people to battle for the destruction of their foe.<div eID="gen24736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go with whirlwinds of the south--</hi>that is, go forth in the most furious storm, such as is one from the south (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">Is 21:1</reference>). Alluding, perhaps, to Jehovah's ancient miracles at Sinai coming "from Teman" ("the south," in the Margin). <div eID="gen24737" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5cd3d20e302e2a668afb9f561ac7f84b2d95c00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13137"/><div sID="gen24738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13137"/><hi type="bold">15. devour--</hi>the flesh of their foes.<div eID="gen24738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drink--</hi>the blood of their foes; that is, utterly destroy them. Image (as <reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">Jr 46:10</reference>) from a sacrifice, wherein part of the flesh was eaten, and the blood poured in libation (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Is 63:1</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen24739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">subdue with sling-stones--</hi>or, "tread under foot the sling-stones" hurled by the foe at them; that is, will contemptuously trample on the hostile missiles which shall fall harmless under their feet (compare <reference osisRef="Job.41.28">Job 41:28</reference>). Probably, too, it is implied that their foes are as impotent as the common stones used in slinging when they have fallen under foot: in contrast to the people of God (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.16">Zec 9:16</reference>), "the (precious) stones of a crown" (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.29">1Sa 25:29</reference>) [Maurer]. English Version is good sense: The Jews shall subdue the foe at the first onset, with the mere slingers who stood in front of the line of battle and began the engagement. Though armed with but sling-stones, like David against Goliath, they shall subdue the foe (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.16">Jud 20:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.2">1Ch 12:2</reference>) [Grotius].<div eID="gen24740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">noise--</hi>the battle shout.<div eID="gen24741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through wine--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.10.7">Zec 10:7</reference>).
